passage: I'm Ankita, and last term my friend Keerthana changed so fast it scared me. She quit chess club, which she loved. She stopped sitting with us at lunch. In the April heat she wore a full-sleeved sweater every day. Then she handed me her whole set of sketch pens and said, "Keep them. I won't need them." Some people in our class group chat were joking that she was being dramatic. I didn't add anything. After school I walked home with her and said I'd noticed, and that I cared. She shrugged and said nothing was going to get better anyway. That scared me even more. I went straight back to school and found Ms Fernandes, our class teacher. She listened, thanked me, and phoned Keerthana's parents and the school counsellor before I'd even left the staffroom. Keerthana is getting help now. We're still friends.

qa.q: What did Keerthana give Ankita?
qa.a: Her whole set of sketch pens.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana's shrug and words scare Ankita even more?
qa.a: Saying nothing was going to get better sounded hopeless, so Ankita feared Keerthana might be in real danger.

qa.q: Which choice did Ankita make instead of joining the group-chat jokes?
qa.a: Ankita spoke to Keerthana privately with care, then went straight to the class teacher that same afternoon.

qa.q: How might Keerthana have felt when Ankita said it had been noticed and that someone cared?
qa.a: Keerthana may have felt seen rather than mocked, even without being able to say much back.

grounding: It shows a friend noticing withdrawal, a sweater in the heat, giving things away and hopeless talk, and choosing caring attention and a teacher over gossip.

passage:
Coach's note, under-16 hockey squad, Tuesday. Coach Raghav.
For three weeks Jaya has skipped the warm-up jokes she usually leads and sat alone on the bench. Today she was suddenly bright and calm, and after practice she handed her new stick to a junior and said, "You'll use it more than me." She also had a bandaged wrist she wouldn't explain. Two players were whispering about it; I told them to stop, and to come to me whenever they're worried about a teammate.
What I did next: I asked Jaya to help me carry cones, and in the storeroom I told her what I'd noticed. I asked plainly whether she was thinking of hurting herself. She was quiet, then said, "Sometimes." I stayed with her, thanked her for telling me, and phoned the school counsellor, who came over within the hour. Her mother arrived soon after, and they went together to the counsellor's office.

qa.q: What did Jaya hand to a junior?
qa.a: Her new stick.

qa.q: What worried Raghav about Jaya's sudden brightness?
qa.a: Raghav felt worried because, after three weeks of withdrawal, the sudden calm and giving away her new stick felt to Raghav like warning signs, not recovery.

qa.q: What was the key choice Raghav made in the storeroom?
qa.a: Raghav asked plainly whether Jaya was thinking of hurting herself, stayed with her and phoned the school counsellor at once.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jaya to be asked plainly in the storeroom?
qa.a: Jaya may have felt some relief at finally being seen; her quiet "Sometimes" suggests she had not been able to say it before.

grounding: It shows a coach noticing withdrawal, a sudden mood change, giving things away and an unexplained injury, and responding with care instead of letting gossip spread.

passage:
Tuesday night
Something's not right with Parveen. This week she gave me her favourite bracelet and her whole shelf of novels. She said, "I won't need them." She's stopped coming to lunch. It's so hot and she keeps wearing full sleeves. Some girls in class were whispering about her, and I told them to stop.
At break I found her alone by the water tank. I said, "I've noticed you're not yourself. I'm worried about you." She said, "I'm just tired of everything. Nothing's going to get better."
I didn't leave her. I said, "Come with me," and we went to Ms Fernandes, the counsellor, right then. Ms Fernandes kept her there and called her mother, who came to school before the last bell.
Vinita

qa.q: What did Parveen give Vinita this week?
qa.a: Her favourite bracelet and her whole shelf of novels.

qa.q: How did Vinita feel about the changes in Parveen?
qa.a: Vinita felt worried and uneasy, sensing something was not right and wanting to help rather than gossip.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that showed caring attention?
qa.a: Vinita stopped the whispering, spoke to Parveen privately, stayed with her and took her to the counsellor at once, who called her mother that day.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt when Vinita said she was worried?
qa.a: Parveen may have felt noticed and less alone, even while feeling hopeless and tired.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing withdrawal, giving things away, covered arms and hopeless talk, responding with caring attention and getting adult help the same day instead of gossip.

passage:
Kalyani: you can have my guitar. I'm not going to play it any more
Pradeep: what? you love that guitar
Kalyani: doesn't matter
Pradeep: you deleted all your photos too. and you've skipped school all week
Pradeep: I'm really worried about you
Kalyani: it's not like it matters what happens to me
Pradeep: can I ask you straight? are you thinking of hurting yourself?
Kalyani: sometimes. yeah
Pradeep: thank you for telling me. I'm coming over right now. I'm not leaving you alone
Pradeep: I'm calling your mum on the way. is that ok?
Kalyani: ok
Pradeep reached her gate in ten minutes. He sat with Kalyani on the steps while her mother came running out, and together they called the helpline.

qa.q: What did Kalyani offer to give Pradeep?
qa.a: Kalyani offered Pradeep the guitar.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel reading Kalyani's messages?
qa.a: Pradeep felt worried and alarmed, noticing the giving away, deleted photos and hopeless words.

qa.q: What did Pradeep do that was right?
qa.a: He asked directly, thanked Kalyani for telling, went over immediately, didn't leave, told Kalyani's mother and called the helpline together.

qa.q: How might Kalyani have felt when Pradeep said he was coming over?
qa.a: Kalyani may have felt less alone and a little relieved that someone took the words seriously.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing giving things away, withdrawal and hopeless talk, asking with care and making sure a trusted adult and helpline are involved at once.

passage: In the village, the boys had started whispering that Yash had "gone mad." He'd quit cricket, given his cycle to his little cousin, and snapped at anyone who spoke to him. Twice Sahil had seen fresh marks on his forearm that Yash wouldn't explain. Sahil, fifteen, told the others to shut up. After school he caught up with Yash by the canal. "You've changed a lot. I'm not here to tease. I'm worried." Yash stared at the water. "Nothing matters any more." Sahil didn't argue, and he didn't leave. "Walk with me to Masterji's house. Now." Masterji listened quietly, thanked Yash for coming, and sent for his parents and the health worker that same evening. Sahil waited on the verandah until they came.

qa.q: What did Yash give to his little cousin?
qa.a: He gave his cycle to his little cousin.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel when the boys whispered that Yash had gone mad?
qa.a: Sahil felt uncomfortable and protective, telling them to shut up instead of joining the gossip.

qa.q: What did Sahil do that was wise?
qa.a: He spoke to Yash privately with care, stayed with him and took him to a trusted adult that same day, who involved his parents and the health worker.

qa.q: How might Yash have felt when Sahil said he wasn't there to tease?
qa.a: Yash may have felt cautious but relieved that someone cared rather than gossiped.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing withdrawal, giving things away, unexplained injuries and hopeless talk, choosing care over gossip and bringing in a trusted adult the same day.

passage:
Amara had known Leila since Year 7 at their school in Leeds, so she noticed when things changed. Leila stopped sitting with the group at lunch. She wore long sleeves through the hot June week. One day she said, flatly, "It won't matter soon anyway." On Thursday she gave Amara her favourite denim jacket. "You have it. I don't need it."
In the toilets, two girls were whispering about Leila. Amara didn't join in. Her stomach felt tight with worry.
She went straight to Mr Hughes, the safeguarding lead, before the last lesson. "I'm worried about Leila. She's giving her things away and saying it won't matter soon."
Mr Hughes put his pen down at once. "Thank you for telling me. You did the right thing." He found Leila that afternoon, sat with her in his office, and called her parents before she went home.

qa.q: What did Leila give Amara on Thursday?
qa.a: Her favourite denim jacket.

qa.q: How did Amara feel as she noticed the changes in Leila?
qa.a: She felt worried and uneasy, her stomach tight, especially after the jacket and the hopeless remark.

qa.q: What did Amara do that others could learn from?
qa.a: She ignored the gossip and told the safeguarding lead the same day, describing exactly what she had seen and heard.

qa.q: What might it be like for Leila when Mr Hughes sits with her?
qa.a: She may feel scared or exposed at first, and perhaps also relieved that someone noticed and cared.

grounding: Amara notices a friend's withdrawal, hopeless talk, giving things away and big changes, and responds with caring action rather than gossip or ignoring.
